# Introduction

Text classification involves assigning predefined categories to text.  For our project we’ll be fine-tuning a pre-trained large language model (llm) from Hugging Face for use in predicting sentiment on unseen data. Sentiment analysis is where text is labeled based on its emotional tone. The pre-trained model will be fine-tuned on a  dataset of New York Times comments from the 2017 year.  This dataset has already had each comment labeled as negative, neutral, or positive from a previous project.  Once the pre-trained model has been fine-tuned, we will use it to predict sentiment of unlabeld comments from the New York Times 2018 dataset. Unlabeld means that there are no sentiments assigned to any of the rows.

First we’ll review what a pre-trained model is.  A LLM is trained on a broad dataset to learn general patterns.  Basically through this process is where model parameters and weights are learned.  It can be a time consuming process thus fine-tuning  a pre-trained model on specific data to adapt it for specialized tasks saves time.

## Tokenize

Tokenization breaks text into manageable units or tokens. Tokenization helps pre-process text data, simplifying tasks such as filtering out punctuation, converting to lowercase, and handling special characters. It also transforms text into numerical IDs which transformers and LLMs require. Tokenization has different methods such as splitting text into individual words,splitting words into sub-words, and breaking text into individual characters. For our model we will split our data into individual words.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"


tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("cardiffnlp/twitter-roberta-base-sentiment-latest")


```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"


def tokenize(batch):
    temp = tokenizer(batch['text'], padding="max_length", truncation=True, max_length=514)
    return temp



```

Apply the function to the dataset

## Labels

There is one last step needed to prepare our data. As will be seen later when setting up the configuration, the model requires two variables: label2id and id2label. This was mentioned when reviewing the initial dataset: the requirement of a label_name column and label column for creating these variables.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"



dataset['train'][0]

```

From the output we see the label_name and label columns. We will use list comprehension to create these variables. A list comprehension is a concise way to create a list from another list.

First, label2id will be created. The list comprehension will create a dictionary with key/value pairs. Label_name is the key and label is the value. Basically, this is mapping label_name to label.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"

label2id = {x['label_name']:x['label'] for x in dataset['train']}


```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"


label2id.items()

```

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| echo: false


label2id

```

label2id has been successfully created as seen in the output.

Now we will use label2id to create id2label. The difference in using list comprehension for creating id2label is the key/value pairs will be interchanged and the key from label2id becomes values and values become keys. This results in id2label having label as the key and label_name as the values.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"

id2label = {v:k for  k,v in label2id.items()}


```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"

id2label.items()


```

## Metrics

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| echo: false


accuracy = evaluate.load("accuracy")
precision = evaluate.load("precision")
recall = evaluate.load("recall")
f1 = evaluate.load("f1")


```

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| echo: false


accuracy.features

```

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| echo: false



def compute_metrics(eval_pred):
    predictions, labels = eval_pred
    predictions = np.argmax(predictions, axis=1)
    accuracy=accuracy.compute(predictions=predictions, references=labels)["accuracy"]
    precision=precision.compute(predictions=predictions, references=labels)["precision"]
    recall=recall.compute(predictions=predictions, references=labels)["recall"]
    f1=f1.compute(predictions=predictions, references=labels)["f1"]
    return {"accuracy":accuracy, "precision":precision, "recall":recall, "f1":f1}


```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"


from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score




```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"

def compute_metrics(pred):
    labels = pred.label_ids
    preds = pred.predictions.argmax(-1)

    acc = accuracy_score(labels, preds)
    prec = precision_score(labels, preds, average='weighted')
    rec = recall_score(labels, preds, average='weighted')
    f1 = f1_score(labels, preds, average='weighted')

    return {"accuracy": acc, "precision": prec, "recall": rec, "f1": f1}




```

The function creates the computation of our selected metrics forf use during the model evaluation on our validation set.

Metric definition:

• Accuracy-measures the number of predictions that are correct as a percentage of the total number of predictions that are made. As an example, if 90% of your predictions are correct, your accuracy is simply 90%. Calculation: number of correct predictions/Number of total predictions. TP+TN/(TP+TN+FP+FN) • Precision-tells us about the quality of positive predictions. It may not find all the positives but the ones that the model does classify as positive are likely to be correct. As an example, out of everyone predicted to have defaulted, how many of them did default? So, within everything that has been predicted as positive, precision counts the percentage that is correct. Calculation: True positives/All Positives. TP/(TP+FP) • Recall- tells us about how well the model identifies true positives. The model may find a lot of positives, yet it also will incorrectly detect many positives that are not actually positives. Out of all the patients who have the disease, how many were correctly identified? So, within everything that is positive, how many did the model successfully find? A model with low recall is unable to find all (or a large part) of the positive cases in the data. Calculated as: True Positives/ (False Negatives + True Positives) • F1 Score-The F1 score is defined as the harmonic mean of precision and recall. The formula for the F1 score is the following: 2 times(precision\*Recall)/ (Precision + Recall)) Since the F1 score is an average of Precision and Recall, it means that the F1 score gives equal weight to Precision and Recall.

Rhe definitions are also relevent for our interpreting results of the classification report from the test set.

These metrics

## Configure Training Arguments

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"



training_args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="./results",
    overwrite_output_dir=True,
    eval_strategy="epoch",
    save_strategy="epoch",
    learning_rate=2e-5,
    per_device_train_batch_size=16,
    per_device_eval_batch_size=16,
    num_train_epochs=3,
    weight_decay=0.01,
    logging_dir="./logs",
    logging_first_step=10,
    save_steps=500,
    disable_tqdm=False


)


```

Training Arguments:

-   Output_dir: the directory where we will store the results of the model.

-   overwrite_ouput_dir: When set to true, the output directory is overwritten on a new training of the model.

-    eval_strategy: The interval for evaluating the model. For our training we have set it to evaluate after each epoch.

-   save_strategy: How often to save the model. We have set it to after each epoch.

-    learning_rate: controls how quickly the model's parameters move towards the optimal solution (minimizing the loss function)

-   per_device_train_batch: subset of the entire training dataset. It is the number of samples processed before the model is updated. per_device_eval_batch_size: is the number of samples processed before the model is evaluated.

-   weight_decay: used to discourage model from using large weight values during training. Prevents overfitting.

-    logging_dir: directory where the logs are saved.

-   save_steps: Determines how frequently the model's checkpoint is saved during training.

Note-An epoch is a training iteration during which we update the paramters for all our training samples.

This time we changed the number of epochs to 3 and reduced the learning rate to 1e-5. The result was a training loss loss of 0.325 and an evaluation loss of 0.40. Though the training loss was lower, the training loss significant increased. We would like to have loss scores below 0.2. Additionally, accuracy, precision, recall, and f1 scores dropped to around 0.85. Lowering the learning rate did not have a positive affect on the model. The issue could be our training data is too small which leads to the model memorizing the training data's specific patterns which causes the model to generalize to new data.

The confusion matrix is a visual representation of how our model performed on predicting on the test set. It shows how many predictions were correct (True Negatives/Neutrals/Positives,) versus incorrect (False Negatives/Neutrals) when compared to actual outcomes.

```{python}
plt.xlabel("Predicted")

#cbar=False,

```

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| echo: false


plt.show()

```

Let's interpret the confusion matrix. The target variable has three values: Negative, Neutral, or Positive The columns represent the actual values of the target variable The rows represent the predicted values of the target variable.

Terms for confusion matrix:

We should note that most confusion matrices have just a positive and negative class. Our model has three classes with neutral being the additional class.

True Positive (TP)

```         
The predicted value matches the actual value.
The actual value was positive, and the model predicted a positive value.
```

True Negative (TN)

```         
The predicted value matches the actual value
The actual value was negative, and the model predicted a negative value.
```

True Neutral (TL)

```         
The predicted value matches the actual value
The actual value was neutral, and the model predicted a neutral value.
```

False Positive (FP)

```         
The predicted value was falsely predicted.
The actual value was negative or neutral, but the model predicted a  positive value.
```

False Negative (FN)

```         
The predicted value was falsely predicted.
The actual value was neutral or positive, but the model predicted a negative value.
```

False Neutral (FL)

```         
The predicted value was falsely predicted.
The actual value was negative or positive, but the model predicted a neutral value.
```

Appyling these terms to our confusion matrix we find:

True Negative (TN) = 16,342, meaning our model correctly classified 16,342 negative class data points. True Neutral (TL) = 5,191, meaning our model correctly classified 5,191 neutral class data points. True Positive (TP) = 15,849, meaning our model correctly classified 15,849 positve class data points. False Negative (FN) = 267,72, meaning the model incorrectly classified 267 neutral and 72 positive class data points as belonging to the negative class. False Neutral (FL) = 368,238, meaning the model incorrectly classified 368 negative and 238 positive class data points as belonging to the neutral class. False Positive (FP) =

We can put these numbers in perspective by using percentages for total predictions for each class.

Of the total predictions for the negative class, 98% were correctly predicted as the negative class, 2% were incorrectly predicted as the neutral class and less than 1% were incorrectly predicted as the positive class.

Of the total predictions for the neutral class, 89% were correctly predicted as the neutral class, 6% were incorrectly predicted as the negative class, and 4% were incorrectly predicted as the positive class.

Of the total predictions for the positive class, 97% were correctly predicted as the positive class, less than 1% were incorrectly predicted as the negative class, and 2% were incorrectly predicted as the neutral class.

The insight we gain from these results is the model is excellent at predicting positive and negative sentiment. The model is not as strong at predicting the neutral class though the results are still considered good.

```{python}
def get_prediction(text):

    input_encoded = tokenizer(text, return_tensors='pt').to(device)

    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = model(**input_encoded)

    logits = outputs.logits
    probabilities = torch.nn.functional.softmax(logits, dim=-1)

    pred = torch.argmax(probabilities, dim=-1).item()
    return probabilities, id2label[pred]
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show Code"




def get_prediction(text):

    """
        Applies fine-tuned model and tokenizer to predict sentiment

        Args: 
            text: A string of text.

        Returns: 
            probabilites: predicted probability of each sentiment. Probabilites sum to 1.
            id2label[pred]: predicted sentiment label.
    """

    input_encoded = new_tokenizer(text, return_tensors='pt').to(device)

    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = new_model(**input_encoded)

    logits = outputs.logits
    probabilities = torch.nn.functional.softmax(logits, dim=-1)

    pred = torch.argmax(probabilities, dim=-1).item()
    return probabilities, id2label[pred]


```

We created a function that will take in a string of text and return the probabilities of the predicted sentiments and the predicted sentiment label with the highest probability. Probabilty is the confidence we have in predicted label.

For comparison, we will print the text string predicted along with the model output.

# Final

Our fine-tuned model can be used in a number of ways. We can build a streamlit application with our model which will allow users to have a user interface to upload text for sentiment prediction. Our model can also be used as part of an AI Agent.
